# Fast Release, Deep Verification, and deployment

## Current workflow coverage (2026-10-22)

`Fast Release` is the application release lane for API, Worker, and Web. It runs frozen dependency installation, workspace build, lint, tests, CI helper tests, performance policy tests, parallel application image builds, and the real web-first Compose smoke. A successful `main` run publishes exactly `API_IMAGE`, `WORKER_IMAGE`, and `WEB_IMAGE` as immutable GHCR digest references for one commit. Pull requests verify and smoke but never publish. A newer commit may cancel an older Fast Release because this workflow never mutates Coolify or Production.

`Deep Verification` retains browser and platform regression, recovery drills, capacity checks, evidence upload, and four infrastructure-aware image builds: API, Worker, Web, and PostgreSQL backup. It runs nightly, manually, and for protected infrastructure changes. Any infrastructure change under CI workflows/helpers, infrastructure smoke scripts, backup contexts, or deployment Compose requires Deep Verification and is intentionally prevented from producing a Fast Release-ready summary. Deep Verification is non-cancellable once started.

The PostgreSQL backup image used by Fast Release is built locally as an isolated smoke fixture and is not published by that lane. For an application-only release, keep `POSTGRES_IMAGE` unchanged. PostgreSQL backup image promotion must use the output from a successful Deep Verification run. EMQX is a separate Git-backed Coolify resource and is not published as an application image.

Production deployment remains manual. Copy the complete `API_IMAGE`, `WORKER_IMAGE`, and `WEB_IMAGE` set from one successful Fast Release summary into the existing Coolify resource and redeploy it without recreating volumes. The optional `Deploy Staging` workflow is also manual, requires all immutable digest inputs and the current `main` SHA, and has non-cancelling deployment concurrency. No Fast Release job receives Coolify credentials.

Only commit-SHA tags are used for discovery; deployment references must be `ghcr.io/...@sha256:...`. A partially pushed failed run is not release-ready. Rollback means restoring all three previous application digests together and redeploying the existing resource after checking schema compatibility.

Customer/site fixtures use explicit domain grants and site-account assignments. Integration preserves MQTT commit acknowledgements, duplicate replay, restart durability, authorization boundaries, telemetry persistence, document evidence, and desktop/mobile UI. Deep checks run only against disposable stacks and upload allowlisted logs/screenshots, never account fixtures or production secrets.

## CI browser preparation and phase timings

The Ubuntu verification pipeline runs the browser in a separate CI-only container using Playwright 1.63.0, matching the installed web workspace package. Following the multi-job parallel acceleration (ADR 0042), both `verify-platform` (for browser smokes, integration and regression) and `drills-capacity` (for mixed-workload browser latency measurements in `platform-load.sh`) manage independent version-matched browser server instances. Each job pulls `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.63.0-noble@sha256:bc6ab0d6d44ff4826e4cb8c1e6d801e185bfc42bb0753f8e2a30efc70db054c7` for `linux/amd64`; the digest was verified against the registry manifest. The image supplies Chromium and its OS libraries; startup installs the exact `playwright@1.63.0` npm server package. Package and image versions must be updated together. A mismatch fails before pulling.

`scripts/ci/browser-server.sh start` uses a unique run/attempt/job name and ownership label, host networking, host IPC and an init process. The server binds only `127.0.0.1:13999`; readiness uses a real Playwright connection and is bounded to 60 seconds. The preparation step has a five-minute limit, including registry and npm access. `CI_BROWSER_WS_ENDPOINT=ws://127.0.0.1:13999/` is exported only after readiness for integration, platform and capacity browser suites. In `drills-capacity`, browser preparation runs immediately before `platform-load.sh`, avoiding unnecessary container idle time during the 190-second fault-injection pause in `recovery-drill.sh`. The client passes Chromium's supported localhost-to-IPv4 resolver launch argument, preserving existing localhost cookie origins on the host network. `run-server --unsafe` permits this argument on the loopback-only CI listener. Local tests keep their ordinary Chromium launch unless this CI endpoint is explicitly configured. No production image or deployment configuration includes the browser service.

Always-run cleanup checks the ownership label, captures `test/artifacts/browser-server.log`, and removes only that browser container; existing fixture cleanup remains in each suite. Browser logs join the uploaded test/drill evidence. Pull/start/readiness failures are reported by browser preparation, independently of application suite failures.

The job summary records UTC start/end timestamps, elapsed seconds and exit status for browser preparation, application image build, integration, platform regression, recovery, capacity and GHCR publication. The timing wrapper preserves failing commands' exit status, so publication still requires all existing gates. Skipped phases have no timing row; a runner forcibly terminating the process can prevent its final row from being recorded. Queue time and optional Coolify deployment are outside these verification phase durations. Application image build, integration, platform regression, recovery, capacity and publication have individual limits of 10, 8, 15, 12, 10 and 10 minutes respectively, with the existing 45-minute verification limit retained. These bounds expose stuck phases without relaxing their assertions. Recovery emits fixed phase names and Compose operation/service start/end timestamps and status; command arguments, SQL and captured successful output are excluded from progress logs. Its intentional 190-second backup pause and all restore/refusal gates remain intact.

Performance validation remains pending: no complete Linux browser run or three comparable main/manual workflow runs were dispatched for this change. Collect at least three successful equivalent runs, including a cold browser-image pull, report each phase duration and the median, and compare against a completed baseline before claiming acceleration. Record queue and Coolify deployment separately. The supplied failed run from 2026-10-06 spent approximately 21m03s installing browser dependencies, 4m21s building images, 1m25s in integration, 7m18s in platform regression, 5m22s in recovery, and 2m10s in capacity (step-start boundaries, including transition overhead). It reached evidence upload after about 44m39s and did not publish. Excluding the old browser installation still leaves about 23m36s: a 10–15 minute verification/publication target is unsupported by this baseline. Browser-container preparation and the capacity implementation need new measurements; there is no verified end-to-end speedup yet. If preparation hits five minutes, diagnose registry/npm access before adding caching.

## Deployment layout

For new pilot deployments, use separate [website](../docs/runbooks/coolify-web-first-deployment-th.md) and [MQTT](../docs/runbooks/coolify-mqtt-deployment-th.md) resources. Deploy Production manually using immutable CI digests. The manual `Deploy Staging` workflow supports only the combined `docker-compose.staging.yml` layout; it does not orchestrate split resources or update `POSTGRES_IMAGE`. The one-time setup below is for that combined layout.

## One-time setup

1. Protect `main`: require pull requests and successful `Fast Release / Fast Verification (Unit, Lint, Build)`; require `Deep Verification` for protected infrastructure changes; disallow force pushes. Do not configure `pull_request_target` execution of PR code.
2. Create a GitHub environment named `staging`, restrict deployment branches to `main`. No human approval is required for ordinary successful main runs.
3. Keep Coolify Auto Deploy disabled. Application publication never deploys automatically; run `Deploy Staging` manually only after collecting a complete compatible digest set.
4. Create a Coolify **Git-backed Docker Compose application**, repository `nateekarni/solar-roof`, branch `main`, compose path `/infra/docker/docker-compose.staging.yml`. Configure the required secrets/settings documented beside that compose file. The repository is public, but new GHCR packages start private. For UI-only pulls, the package owner must deliberately make each required package public in GitHub package settings after reviewing the published contents, or use registry access already provisioned by the company. This workflow does not change package visibility. Follow the staging runbook for GitHub and Coolify UI steps.
5. **Disable Coolify Auto Deploy on push and preview deployments.** Remove old unauthenticated deployment webhooks and do not run manual deployments concurrently. The deployment helper also explicitly disables push and preview deployment every run.
6. In the GitHub `staging` environment configure variables `COOLIFY_URL` (HTTPS origin, no `/api/v1` suffix), `COOLIFY_APPLICATION_UUID`, `STAGING_WEB_URL` (public HTTPS origin, normally `https://solar.fowir.com`). Add secret `COOLIFY_API_TOKEN` with Coolify application read/write and deployment permissions restricted to the staging team/resource where supported. Never put this token in repository files, URLs, or frontend variables. Restrict API access to the runner/network policy suitable for your Coolify installation.
7. Configure DB/storage/JWT secrets before deployment. There is no automatic bootstrap user service. After migration, run `pnpm --filter @solar/api db:create:user` explicitly in the API terminal for each role as described in [manual users](../docs/runbooks/coolify-manual-users-th.md). No demo seed data is loaded and rerunning preserves compatible existing passwords. Configure the separate EMQX resource and its host-mounted MQTTS certificate using the MQTT runbook.

## Deployment contract and failure recovery

Before any API request, the helper validates the three registry-specific application digest references. Before mutation, CI rejects stale commits that no longer equal main. The helper verifies the application's UUID, repository, main branch, compose build pack and staging compose path; it rejects an already active deployment. The helper PATCHes the application's tested `git_commit_sha`, disables raw push deployment, updates `API_IMAGE`, `WORKER_IMAGE`, and `WEB_IMAGE` via the authenticated bulk environment API, then POSTs `/deploy`. It polls the returned matching deployment UUID, rejects failed/cancelled deployments, and verifies the final commit equals the tested SHA. Finally CI probes web login and web health. The private API readiness check runs inside the Coolify stack; no public API port is needed. It never prints API response bodies/tokens, follows redirects with credentials, or retries deployment-triggering POSTs.

Deep Verification and staging deployment concurrency have `cancel-in-progress: false`: a new push cannot kill a drill or migration. Fast Release is separately cancellable and never deploys. A timeout does not cancel the Coolify deployment. Inspect Coolify and wait for the active deployment to stop before retrying. Failed readiness leaves the job red; it is not a successful release. Database rollback is never automated. For application rollback use a previously tested commit and restore its three application digests together after checking schema compatibility; back up before migrations that cannot be reversed.

Verified API references: [application update](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/applications/update-application-by-uuid), [bulk environment update](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/applications/update-envs-by-application-uuid), [deploy](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/deployments/deploy-by-tag-or-uuid), [deployment status](https://coolify.io/docs/api/endpoints/deployments/get-deployment-by-uuid). These are application endpoints; `docker_compose_raw` is not part of the documented application PATCH schema, so this workflow deploys the compose file from the pinned commit.

Local equivalents: `node --test scripts/ci/*.test.mjs`, build `solar-api:ci`, `solar-worker:ci`, `solar-web:ci`, and `solar-postgres-backup:ci` from their matching Dockerfiles, then run `bash scripts/ci/integration.sh`. The integration fixture uses EMQX and disposable local services. These checks require Docker, pnpm, and Playwright Chromium. CI accounts and passwords are deliberately limited to the disposable `solar_readiness` database and localhost ports.

## Production finance acceptance

`integration.sh` and the `financial-core` suite in `platform-check.sh all-fast --prebuilt` run `apps/api/test/production-financial-workflow.integration.ts` against the owned disposable CI database, object storage and real Mailpit. `finance-readiness` is an alias for a focused run. This implements the previously pending financial-core gate. The overlay `infra/ci/production-finance.yml` publishes only loopback SMTP 11025, Mailpit 18026 and Redis 16432. Financial flags are enabled only in the acceptance process; the ordinary CI API keeps its default-off financial configuration.

The test creates a random `task9_<uuid>` schema from the migrated table definitions and application triggers, seeds two controlled sites and three accounts, then runs actual Owner browser setup, invoice/payment/receipt delivery and scheduler/cutover replay. It asserts 1,000 kWh × 4.3210 plus explicit 7% tax = THB 4,623.47, hashes the stored originals and actual Mailpit attachments, and checks frozen snapshots after branding changes. An incomplete site remains blocked independently. Browser checks include logo upload, loading/login/sidebar branding, confirmation and role boundaries, and the downloaded original's header geometry. The application processes stop before the schema is dropped, and the unique storage evidence object is removed in `finally`.

Build the workspace before clean-checkout web tests (`pnpm build`, then lint/test). The acceptance launcher uses that production Next build and the existing version-matched browser transport. Local Windows verification may set `PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH` to its installed browser; hosted CI uses `browser-server.sh` and `CI_BROWSER_WS_ENDPOINT`.

Safe evidence is written to `test/artifacts/production-finance.json`, `production-*.pdf`, and `production-finance-browser*.json`/`.png`. The workflow uploads only those allowlisted outputs. The local browser fixture/runtime JSON contains synthetic login material and database access details; it is excluded from artifact uploads and removed by the disposable runner even on failure. Do not stage generated evidence or environment files.
